title: Pappardelle ai Funghi Misti
subtitle: pappardelle with mixed wild mushrooms in white wine and herbs
excerpt: Pappardelle ai funghi misti pairs wide ribbons of egg pasta with a white-wine-braised mix of wild and cultivated mushrooms, finished with thyme, parsley, and Parmesan. It is a fuller, more rustic dish than the cream-based version. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Pappardelle are wide egg ribbon noodles from Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna. The pairing of pappardelle with mushrooms (funghi misti, or mixed mushrooms) is a central Tuscany and Emilia autumn dish. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), gives recipes for mushrooms cooked in olive oil with wine that form the basis of this sauce type. The version without cream, using only wine, stock, and olive oil to braise the mushrooms, produces a cleaner, more intensely mushroom-flavoured result.

glossaryTerms.definition: Mixed mushrooms. In autumn in Italy this means whatever combination of wild and cultivated mushrooms is available: porcini, chanterelles (girolles), oyster mushrooms, shiitake, and chestnut mushrooms in varying proportions. A mix gives more complexity than any single variety alone.

Wide ribbon pasta about 2 to 3 cm across, made with egg dough. The width makes pappardelle suited to hearty, chunky sauces that would overwhelm a thinner pasta; the mushroom pieces sit in the ribbon folds rather than sliding off.

content.text: is the cream-free version of mushroom pasta. The mushrooms cook in wine until the liquid reduces and coats them. A splash of pasta water and a quick toss in the pan make a light sauce. The result is deeply savoury and less rich than the cream version, with the mushrooms tasting more clearly of themselves.

Use whatever mushrooms are available. A mix is always better than one variety alone. Dried porcini soaked and added with their liquid add depth to shop-bought cultivated mushrooms. Fresh porcini or chanterelles need less cooking time; add them after the chestnut mushrooms have had their initial browning.

items.prepNote: soaked in 200 ml hot water 20 minutes

content.text: If using dried porcini, soak in 200 ml of hot water for 20 minutes. Lift out, chop roughly, and strain the liquid. Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil for the pasta.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large saute pan over a high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer and leave for 2 to 3 minutes until browned underneath. Turn and cook for 2 more minutes until golden. Season.

Reduce heat to medium. Add {{shallots}} of shallots, {{garlic}} of garlic, and thyme. Cook for 2 minutes. Add {{dry-white-wine}} of white wine, the porcini and their liquid if using, and {{stock-vegetable}} of stock. Simmer until reduced by half, about 5 minutes.

Cook {{pasta-fresh}} of pappardelle according to the packet. Reserve 150 ml pasta water. Drain and add to the mushroom pan with {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and a splash of pasta water. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute. Add {{parmesan}} of parmesan and {{parsley-flat}} of parsley. Season and serve.

items.symptom: Sauce is too reduced and dry
items.fix: Add pasta water and toss. A knob of butter also loosens the sauce and adds gloss.

items.cause: Not browned properly, or only one variety used
items.fix: Brown is flavour. Let the mushrooms colour properly before adding liquid. Use dried porcini to boost depth.

content.text: Pappardelle with mushrooms is quintessential autumn Tuscan and Emilian cooking. The wide pasta absorbs a robust, savoury sauce in a way that thin pasta cannot. In Tuscany this dish often appears at the start of the porcini season, when foragers bring back their first baskets. It is the kind of dish that appears at family Sunday lunches in towns like Siena, Arezzo, and Modena in October and November, made with whatever combination of fresh and dried mushrooms is to hand.
